examples.en: I want to express my thanks to those who helped.

examples.ko: 저는 부모님의 고마움을 요즘 많이 느껴요.
examples.en: I've been feeling a lot of gratitude toward my parents lately.
My gratitude is big, so I prepared a small gift.
I'm shy about saying my thanks to my friend.
I wrote my feeling of thanks at the end of the letter.

examples.ko: 그때의 고마움은 평생 잊지 못할 거예요.
examples.en: I will never forget my gratitude from that time.

explain: '고맙다'는 말하는 순간의 감정이고, 고마움은 그 마음 자체를 명사로 말할 때 써요. '고마움을 느끼다/전하다/표현하다'처럼 같이 써요. 비슷한 '감사'는 더 격식 있고 공식적인 자리에 어울려요.
explain_en: 고맙다 expresses the feeling in the moment, while 고마움 names that feeling as a noun. Typical verbs: 고마움을 느끼다/전하다/표현하다. 감사 is the more formal, official counterpart.

examples.ko: 저는 글쓰기를 좋아해서 매일 일기를 써요.
examples.en: I like writing, so I keep a diary every day.
Writing gets easier the more you practice.
Korean writing is still hard for me.
I take a writing class at school.
It's good to start with short pieces of writing.
I stayed up all night because of the writing homework.

explain: 한국어 시험이나 수업에서 '말하기, 듣기, 읽기, 쓰기'를 나눌 때 보통 '쓰기'라고 해요. 글쓰기는 글을 쓰는 활동 전체를 가리켜서 '글쓰기 수업', '글쓰기 연습'처럼 써요. '글쓰기를 하다'보다 '글을 쓰다'가 말로는 더 자연스러워요.
explain_en: In tests and classes the skill is usually called 쓰기 (alongside 말하기, 듣기, 읽기). 글쓰기 refers to the activity of writing in general, as in 글쓰기 수업 or 글쓰기 연습. In speech, 글을 쓰다 sounds more natural than 글쓰기를 하다.

dis.h: act of composing essays or text

p.n: The swap sounds like the school skill rather than the creative act of composing.

examples.en: I always read before I go to bed.
I read at a quiet cafe on the weekend.

examples.ko: 독서하는 시간이 하루 중에 제일 행복해요.
examples.en: Reading time is the happiest part of my day.
During vacation I want to spend the whole day reading.

examples.ko: 동생은 매일 한 시간씩 독서하기로 했어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling decided to read for an hour every day.

examples.ko: 올해 독서한 책 중에 이 책이 제일 좋았어요.
examples.en: Of the books I read this year, this one was the best.

explain: 대화에서는 '책을 읽어요'가 훨씬 자연스러워요. '독서'는 '취미가 독서예요'처럼 명사로 쓰거나 '독서를 하다'로 많이 말해요. 신문이나 메시지처럼 책이 아닌 것에는 '독서'를 안 쓰고 '읽다'를 써요.

phrases.example: 동생이 독서삼매경에 빠져서 제가 불러도 몰라요.
phrases.nuance_ko: 책에 푹 빠져서 다른 소리가 안 들릴 정도일 때 써요. 보통 '빠지다'와 함께 말해요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when someone is so lost in a book that they don't hear anything else. It usually goes with the verb '빠지다' (to fall into).

explain_en: In conversation, '책을 읽어요' sounds much more natural. 독서 is mostly used as a noun, as in '취미가 독서예요' (my hobby is reading), or as '독서를 하다'. For things that aren't books, such as newspapers or messages, use '읽다', not 독서.

dis.h: read books as an activity; no object

p.n: The everyday verb needs an object, such as 책을 읽어요.

examples.en: I argued with my friend, so I feel bad.
Yesterday I argued with my younger sibling over a game.
If parents argue often, the child has a hard time too.
Don't argue, let's talk calmly.

examples.ko: 길에서 두 사람이 큰 소리로 말싸움하고 있었어요.
examples.en: Two people were arguing loudly in the street.

examples.ko: 그 일로 또 말싸움할 것 같아서 걱정이에요.
examples.en: I'm worried we'll argue about that again.

explain: '싸우다'보다 말로만 다투는 느낌이 분명해요. '친구와/친구랑 말싸움하다'처럼 같이 하는 사람에게 '와/과, 랑'을 써요. '말싸움을 하다'로 띄어 써도 돼요.
explain_en: It clearly means fighting with words only, more than 싸우다 does. The other person takes 와/과 or 랑, as in '친구랑 말싸움하다'. You can also split it as '말싸움을 하다'.

examples.ko: 그 선수의 슛이 골대를 맞고 나왔어요.
examples.en: That player's shot hit the post and bounced out.
He sank a great shot at the last moment.

examples.ko: 저는 농구에서 슛 연습을 매일 해요.
examples.en: I practice shooting in basketball every day.

examples.ko: 우리 팀은 슛을 열 번이나 쐈지만 못 넣었어요.
examples.en: Our team took ten shots but couldn't score.
When the shot went in, the crowd stood up.
Our team's shooting was weak, so we lost.

explain: 축구·농구·핸드볼에서 공을 골대로 보낼 때 써요. 보통 '슛을 하다', '슛을 쏘다', '슛을 넣다'를 같이 말해요. 응원하는 사람은 '슛!'이라고 소리치기도 해요.
explain_en: Used for sending the ball at the goal in soccer, basketball, and handball. Common verbs: 슛을 하다, 슛을 쏘다, 슛을 넣다. Fans also shout '슛!'.

examples.en: The child is learning the alphabet letter by letter.
The English alphabet has twenty-six letters in all.
Please write your name here in English letters.

examples.ko: 한글과 알파벳은 만든 방법이 많이 달라요.
examples.en: Hangul and the alphabet differ a lot in how they were made.

examples.ko: 이 문서에는 알파벳 순서대로 이름이 있어요.
examples.en: In this document the names are in alphabetical order.
You have to include a capital letter in the password.

explain: 한국에서는 영어의 A, B, C를 말할 때 알파벳이라고 해요. 한글 글자는 '자음'과 '모음'이라고 불러서 알파벳이라고 하지 않아요. 영어 글자는 '에이, 비, 씨'처럼 영어 소리로 읽어요.
explain_en: In Korea 알파벳 refers to A, B, C in English. Hangul letters are called 자음 (consonants) and 모음 (vowels), not 알파벳. The letters are read with English sounds: 에이, 비, 씨.

examples.en: They encouraged customers to visit with a discount.
The teacher draws out the students' answers with questions.
The mart is encouraging return visits with points.

examples.ko: 아이가 스스로 생각하도록 유도하는 게 중요해요.
examples.en: It's important to guide children to think for themselves.
We need a question that eases the conversation along.
Ads are made to lead consumers toward buying.

explain: 억지로 시키지 않고 자연스럽게 원하는 쪽으로 이끈다는 느낌이에요. '참여를 유도하다', '구매를 유도하다'처럼 자주 써요. 상대를 속여서 끌어내는 '유인하다'는 더 부정적으로 들려요.
explain_en: It carries the feeling of steering someone toward what you want naturally, without forcing. Common patterns are '참여를 유도하다' and '구매를 유도하다'. '유인하다', which means luring someone out, sounds more negative.

dis.h: steer someone toward a desired result

p.n: 안내하다 doesn't fit with 'questions' as the object; 유도하다 means to draw something out.
